title: National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence #AIforAll
issuing_body: NITI Aayog
summary: Discussion paper mandated by the Union Budget 2018-19 laying the foundational vision for India's AI strategy under the #AIforAll theme. Frames AI as a tool for inclusive growth and positions India as an AI garage for the world solving complex problems at scale. Focuses on five core sectors: healthcare and agriculture and education and smart cities and smart mobility. Makes recommendations across four areas: promotion of AI research through Centres of Excellence and an umbrella coordinating organisation; skilling and reskilling of the workforce through decentralised teaching and industry collaboration; facilitating adoption of AI solutions in priority sectors; and development of guidelines for responsible AI. Recommends a national data marketplace and annotated sector-specific datasets.
who_it_applies_to: Central ministries and state governments and private sector AI researchers and developers and technology companies
key_obligations: Align national and state programmes to five AI priority sectors and invest in AI research capacity through ICTAI Centres of Excellence and develop annotated datasets for AI in public interest domains and promote international collaboration on AI research

title: Responsible AI for All - Part 1: Guiding Principles
issuing_body: NITI Aayog
summary: First part of NITI Aayog's responsible AI approach document establishing seven core principles for responsible management of AI derived from the Constitution of India: (1) Safety and Reliability; (2) Equality; (3) Inclusivity and Non-discrimination; (4) Privacy and Security; (5) Transparency; (6) Accountability; (7) Protection and Reinforcement of Positive Human Values. Examines seven systems considerations covering AI explainability and consistency and exclusion and accountability and privacy and security risks. Also covers societal considerations, global regulatory landscape, and technology-based approaches. Includes a self-assessment guide for AI usage. Preceded Part 2 on operationalisation of these principles.
who_it_applies_to: Government agencies and AI developers and deployers across public and private sectors
key_obligations: Adopt all seven responsible AI principles during design and development and deployment phases and conduct impact assessments and document AI systems against each principle and apply calibrated measures proportionate to the risk level of the AI application

title: Responsible AI for All - Part 2: Operationalising Responsible AI
issuing_body: NITI Aayog
summary: Second part of the responsible AI approach document providing practical sector-specific guidance on operationalising the seven principles from Part 1 across healthcare and agriculture and MSME and education sectors. Provides case studies and implementation tools including a risk-based assessment framework for responsible AI deployment. Introduces enforcement mechanisms for the RAI principles and sets out the roles of different actors in operationalising them in Indian organisational contexts.
who_it_applies_to: AI developers and deploying organisations across public sector and enterprises using AI in social or governance contexts
key_obligations: Implement sector-specific risk and fairness assessments and use prescribed checklists for AI deployment and establish internal accountability mechanisms and document AI decision trails and apply the enforcement mechanisms specified for each of the seven RAI principles

title: IndiaAI Mission
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MEITY)
summary: Cabinet-approved programme with Rs 10,371.92 crore outlay structured around seven pillars: (1) IndiaAI Compute Capacity — building a high-end scalable AI compute infrastructure of 10,000 or more GPUs for shared subsidised access by startups, researchers, and government entities through a national AI compute portal; (2) IndiaAI Innovation Centre — developing indigenous foundational AI models for key national sectors; (3) IndiaAI Datasets Platform — democratising access to quality non-personal datasets to power AI model development; (4) IndiaAI Application Development Initiative — deploying AI across key sectors including healthcare, agriculture, education, and governance; (5) IndiaAI FutureSkills — scaling AI skilling programmes through 500 PhD fellowships and integration with FutureSkills Prime and existing ITI and polytechnic networks; (6) IndiaAI Startup Financing — providing risk capital to AI startups from idea stage through fund of funds and direct financing; (7) Safe and Trusted AI — developing indigenous tools, frameworks, and benchmarks to embed safety, ethics, and accountability in AI systems. Implemented by IndiaAI Independent Business Division under Digital India Corporation.
who_it_applies_to: Central government bodies and AI startups and academic and research institutions and deep-tech companies
key_obligations: Access shared GPU compute through IndiaAI portal and contribute to IndiaDatasets platform and participate in FutureSkills Prime AI training and apply for startup financing through IndiaAI fund of funds

title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023
issuing_body: Ministry of Law and Justice
summary: Indias primary data protection legislation governing processing of digital personal data. Applies to all entities processing personal data of Indian residents whether in India or abroad while offering goods or services to Indian residents. Establishes rights of Data Principals and obligations of Data Fiduciaries including consent requirements and security safeguards and breach notification and data erasure. Creates the Data Protection Board of India as enforcement authority. Penalties range up to Rs 250 crore for security safeguard breaches.
who_it_applies_to: All Data Fiduciaries (government and private entities) that determine the purpose and means of processing digital personal data of individuals in India or offer goods/services to Indian residents from outside India. Exemptions apply to personal/domestic processing and to processing by state instrumentalities notified by Central Government for sovereignty/security purposes and to research/archiving/statistical uses.
key_obligations: Obtain free and specific and informed and unambiguous consent before processing OR process only for legitimate uses listed in Section 7; give notice describing personal data and purpose before seeking consent; allow withdrawal of consent with ease comparable to how it was given; implement appropriate technical and organisational measures; protect data with reasonable security safeguards to prevent breach; notify Data Protection Board AND each affected Data Principal upon any personal data breach; erase personal data when specified purpose is no longer served or consent is withdrawn; establish grievance redressal mechanism; obtain verifiable parental consent before processing data of children under 18; prohibit tracking and behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children; Significant Data Fiduciaries must additionally appoint India-based Data Protection Officer and independent data auditor and conduct periodic Data Protection Impact Assessments and periodic audits

title: Advisory on Due Diligence and Identification of AI-Generated Deepfakes (December 2023)
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MEITY)
summary: Advisory No. 2(4)/2023-CyberLaws-2 issued by MeitY's Cyber Law and Data Governance Group on 26 December 2023. The advisory directs all intermediaries and platforms to take proactive measures against AI-generated deepfakes and synthetic misinformation. Key directives: (1) platforms must not allow AI-generated content that is unlawful under Rule 3(1)(b) of the IT Rules 2021, including deepfakes or impersonation material; (2) where platforms provide tools for synthetic creation, generation, or modification of text, audio, visual, or audiovisual content that may be used as misinformation or deepfakes, they must embed permanent unique metadata or identifiers enabling attribution to the creator, the first originator, and the platform; (3) intermediaries must ensure AI/ML tools on their platforms do not facilitate bias, discrimination, or threats to electoral integrity. Non-compliance risks loss of safe harbour protection under Section 79 of the IT Act and prosecution. A continuation advisory (No. 2(4)/2023-CyberLaws-3) was issued on 1 March 2024, extending obligations to require labelling of unreliable AI outputs and explicit user consent disclosures.
who_it_applies_to: All intermediaries and platforms operating in India, including social media intermediaries, OTT platforms, messaging services, AI/GenAI tool providers, and online platforms enabling synthetic content generation.
key_obligations: Prevent AI-generated unlawful content (Rule 3(1)(b) IT Rules); embed permanent unique metadata/identifiers in synthetic content for traceability back to creator/originator/platform; prevent AI-enabled bias, discrimination, or threats to electoral integrity; submit action taken report within 15 days of advisory; maintain safe harbour compliance under Section 79 of IT Act 2000.

title: Advisory to Intermediaries on AI Compliance, Unreliable Output Labelling and Deepfake Metadata (March 2024)
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MEITY)
summary: Advisory No. 2(4)/2023-CyberLaws-3 issued by MeitY on 1 March 2024, continuing from the December 2023 deepfakes advisory. Issued in response to observed non-compliance by intermediaries and platforms with IT Rules 2021. The advisory adds four additional compliance requirements: (a) all AI/ML/LLM/GenAI tools deployed on or through any intermediary's computer resource must not allow users to create, upload, or share unlawful content under Rule 3(1)(b) of IT Rules; (b) AI/ML tools must not permit bias, discrimination, or threats to the integrity of the electoral process; (c) under-tested or unreliable AI models made available to Indian internet users must obtain explicit Government of India permission and display a consent popup clearly disclosing the inherent fallibility and unreliability of outputs before deployment; (d) all users must be clearly informed through terms of service and user agreements about the consequences of dealing with unlawful AI-generated information, including suspension or termination of accounts. Platforms with synthetic content tools must embed permanent unique metadata or identifiers enabling attribution of deepfakes or misinformation to their creator and originator. All intermediaries were required to submit an Action Taken cum Status Report to MeitY within 15 days.
who_it_applies_to: All intermediaries and platforms in India hosting, transmitting, or enabling AI/ML/LLM/GenAI functionality, including social media intermediaries, OTT platforms, AI tool providers, GenAI application developers, and any platform that permits synthetic creation or modification of media content.
key_obligations: Prevent unlawful AI-generated content (Rule 3(1)(b) IT Rules); prohibit AI-enabled bias and electoral interference; obtain Government approval before deploying under-tested AI models; display consent popups disclosing AI fallibility; inform users of consequences for unlawful AI content; embed permanent metadata/identifiers in synthetic content for deepfake attribution; submit Action Taken cum Status Report to MeitY within 15 days.

title: Recommendations on Artificial Intelligence and Big Data in Telecom Sector
issuing_body: Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI)
summary: TRAI recommendations covering responsible AI deployment in telecom networks for spectrum management and network optimisation and fraud detection and consumer protection. Recommends a code of conduct for AI in telecom and calls for a dedicated regulatory sandbox and suggests that AI systems used in subscriber-affecting decisions meet explainability standards.
who_it_applies_to: Telecom service providers and equipment vendors and OTT communication services and AI solution providers working with telecom operators
key_obligations: Adopt TRAI-recommended code of conduct for AI use and protect subscriber data in AI systems and register AI use in network management with TRAI and disclose AI-driven decisions affecting consumers

title: Ethical Guidelines for Application of Artificial Intelligence in Biomedical Research and Healthcare
issuing_body: Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)
summary: ICMR guidelines establishing ten patient-centric ethical principles for AI in health: autonomy and safety and privacy and data protection and accessibility and equity and accountability and liability and trustworthiness and optimisation and sustainability and fairness. Covers AI in clinical decision support and diagnostics and drug discovery and public health surveillance. A living document to be updated as the field evolves.
who_it_applies_to: Healthcare AI developers and clinical researchers and hospitals and ethics committees and AI solution vendors and sponsors of AI-in-health research
key_obligations: Obtain independent ethics committee clearance for AI healthcare tools and document training data for bias and ensure patient consent for AI use in care and conduct prospective clinical validation and publish AI audit reports and ensure human oversight in all AI-assisted clinical decisions

title: Telemedicine Practice Guidelines
issuing_body: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) and National Medical Commission
summary: Issued on 25 March 2020 by the Board of Governors (in supersession of Medical Council of India) under the Indian Medical Council (Professional Conduct, Etiquette and Ethics) Regulations 2002, constituting Appendix 5 thereof. India's first legal framework enabling Registered Medical Practitioners (RMPs) to provide healthcare using telemedicine. Defines telemedicine (following WHO definition), telehealth, and establishes that all RMPs are entitled to practice telemedicine subject to completing a mandatory online course. Governs five consultation scenarios: Patient-to-RMP, Caregiver-to-RMP, Health Worker-to-RMP, RMP-to-RMP/Specialist, and emergency situations. Mandates seven elements before any teleconsultation: context assessment, identification of RMP and patient, mode selection (video/audio/text), explicit consent, consultation type (first/follow-up), patient evaluation, and patient management. Establishes a drug prescription matrix with four categories: List O (over-the-counter, any mode), List A (prescription drugs, video first consult only), List B (add-on drugs, follow-up only), and a Prohibited List (Schedule X narcotics/psychotropics — never via telemedicine). Requires RMPs to maintain digital records including consultation logs, patient records, and prescriptions. Data privacy obligations follow IT Act 2000 and applicable rules. Technology platforms enabling telemedicine must verify RMP registration and may not use AI/ML to counsel patients or prescribe medicines — only RMPs may do so. Explicit prohibition: AI/ML-based technology platforms are not allowed to counsel patients or prescribe medicines.
who_it_applies_to: Registered medical practitioners and telemedicine platforms and health-tech companies offering remote consultation and symptom checker services
key_obligations: Verify patient and RMP identity before consultation; obtain explicit or implied patient consent; assess whether telemedicine is appropriate and sufficient; follow drug prescription matrix based on consultation mode and type; prohibit Schedule X and narcotic prescriptions via telemedicine; maintain digital records including consultation logs and prescriptions; uphold medical ethics, data privacy (IT Act 2000), and confidentiality; technology platforms must verify RMP registration and must not enable AI/ML to counsel patients or prescribe.

title: Draft Guidance Document on Medical Device Software
issuing_body: Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO)
summary: Draft CDSCO guidance document for public comment on the regulatory framework for Medical Device Software (MDS) under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 and Medical Devices Rules 2017. Covers two categories: Software in a Medical Device (SiMD) — embedded software that drives or influences hardware medical devices — and Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) — standalone software including AI and ML based diagnostic and clinical decision support tools. Establishes a four-class risk-based classification framework (Class A: low risk through Class D: high risk) using a two-axis matrix combining significance of clinical information provided and seriousness of the healthcare situation. Covers intended use statement requirements and applicable quality standards (IS/ISO 13485 and IS/ISO 14971) and Quality Management System requirements and the regulatory pathway for manufacturing and import licences and clinical investigation requirements and post-market surveillance obligations.
who_it_applies_to: Indian manufacturers and importers of Medical Device Software including developers of AI and ML based diagnostic and therapeutic software and clinical decision support applications; applies to both SaMD and SiMD under MDR-2017
key_obligations: Classify Medical Device Software under appropriate MDR-2017 risk class (A to D) using the prescribed two-axis SaMD risk matrix; submit licence application to Central Licensing Authority or State Licensing Authority per applicable class; provide clinical evidence of safety and performance; implement an ISO 13485 compliant Quality Management System; conduct post-market surveillance and report adverse events within prescribed timelines; obtain CDSCO confirmation of risk classification before commercialisation

title: Reimagining Agriculture: A Roadmap for Frontier Technology Led Transformation
issuing_body: NITI Aayog (Frontier Tech Hub), in collaboration with CII, BCG, Google, and EkStep Foundation
summary: Strategic roadmap published by NITI Aayog's Frontier Tech Hub for integrating frontier technologies into Indian agriculture as part of the Viksit Bharat 2047 vision. Segments India's farming community into three archetypes — Aspiring (70-80%), Transitioning (15-20%), and Advanced (1-2%) — and identifies six systemic roadblocks to technology scale-up: siloed data systems, farmer trust deficits, a phygital divide between digital innovations and physical infrastructure, ecosystem fragmentation, talent gaps, and constrained capital flows. Proposes a Digital Agriculture Mission 2.0 built on three pillars: (1) Enhance — transitioning to a 360-degree sovereign agri data ecosystem (AgriKosh), digitally enabling last-mile advisory through multi-modal AI-powered channels including the VISTAAR platform, and upgrading the AgriTech startup accelerator ecosystem; (2) Reimagine — shifting to mission-oriented translational R&D and building interdisciplinary, industry-aligned talent pipelines across four tiers including AI specialists and drone pilots; (3) Converge — establishing thematic frontier technology Centres of Excellence and institutionalising policy foresight units and regulatory sandboxes for public-private convergence. Covers frontier technologies including agentic AI, precision agriculture, drone and satellite-based field intelligence, digital twins, IoT sensors, and biotech applications. Sets milestone indicators for 2030 and 2047 on yield, irrigation, mechanisation, post-harvest loss reduction, and processing.
who_it_applies_to: Policymakers and central government ministries (MoAFW, MeitY, MSDE, DBT); state agriculture departments; agritech startups and established companies; agricultural universities and research institutions; private investors and accelerators; farmer producer organisations and cooperatives; international development organisations and multilaterals
key_obligations: Non-binding strategic roadmap; recommendations include: government to establish apex interministerial committee for the AgriKosh data ecosystem with MoAFW as domain owner and MeitY for IT governance; national framework to map AgriTech accelerators and track performance; establish time-bound thematic task forces on R&D ecosystem and agri-talent; link sector accelerators to proposed Centres of Excellence; develop national NSQF-aligned agri-talent framework; integrate AI chatbots and extension agent AI co-pilots into a unified multilingual farmer advisory interface; expand use of India's DPI (AgriStack, VISTAAR, ONDC) as infrastructure for agritech innovation

title: Master Direction on Information Technology Governance Risk Controls and Assurance Practices
issuing_body: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
summary: Comprehensive master directions governing IT risk and governance for regulated entities. Contains dedicated provisions for AI and ML model risk management requiring board-level oversight and model inventories and periodic audits and explainability requirements for AI in credit underwriting and fraud scoring. Supersedes earlier IT risk guidelines.
who_it_applies_to: Scheduled commercial banks and primary urban co-operative banks and non-banking financial companies above threshold using technology including AI and ML in customer-facing or operational decisions
key_obligations: Establish board IT strategy committee with AI oversight mandate and maintain AI and ML model inventory with risk classification and conduct annual model audits and implement explainability for AI credit decisions and report AI-related incidents to RBI

title: National Education Policy 2020
issuing_body: Ministry of Education (MoE)
summary: Transformative national education reform recommending integration of coding and AI and computational thinking from Grade 6 and multidisciplinary curricula in higher education. Calls for AI-enabled personalised learning platforms and online course repositories and teacher upskilling in technology pedagogy. Sets vision for India's education system through 2040.
who_it_applies_to: Schools and universities and state education departments and teacher training institutions and education technology companies
key_obligations: Introduce coding and AI literacy from middle school onward and restructure higher education curricula for multidisciplinary learning and train teachers in technology and AI pedagogy and link vocational AI skilling to national credentials

title: CERT-In Advisory on Best Practices for Generative AI Security (CIAD-2025-0013)
issuing_body: Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In)
summary: CERT-In advisory issued in March 2025 identifying key cybersecurity vulnerabilities associated with the use of generative AI solutions and recommending defensive best practices. Covers threat vectors including data poisoning attacks on AI training datasets, adversarial attacks that cause misclassification, model inversion attacks to extract training data, model stealing through repeated querying, prompt injection attacks to bypass content safeguards, hallucination exploitation for disinformation and fraud, and backdoor attacks. Provides practical guidance for organisations and individual users deploying GenAI tools.
who_it_applies_to: All organisations and individuals using generative AI solutions including enterprises deploying AI-powered tools for customer service and logistics and healthcare and cybersecurity functions; AI application developers
key_obligations: Carefully configure access rights of GenAI tools to organisational data and conduct periodic access rights reviews; do not rely on AI alone for critical decisions and fact-check AI outputs against reliable sources; use strong passwords and enable two-factor authentication for AI service accounts; consider anonymous accounts when inputting sensitive information; stay alert for AI-generated phishing and deepfake threats; avoid AI-generated plagiarised content

title: Maharashtra Artificial Intelligence Policy 2025
issuing_body: Government of Maharashtra
summary: Maharashtra's first dedicated AI policy being developed by a 16-member AI Policy Taskforce constituted in January 2025 under the state's IT Ministry. Expected to focus on innovation and job creation and cybersecurity and education and alignment with India's IndiaAI Mission. Maharashtra will be the first Indian state with a standalone dedicated AI policy upon finalisation.
who_it_applies_to: State government departments and enterprises and educational institutions and AI startups in Maharashtra
key_obligations: Details pending finalisation; expected to cover AI sandbox participation and compliance with state data sharing norms and alignment with IndiaAI Mission standards and skilling obligations

title: Telangana Artificial Intelligence Framework 2020
issuing_body: Government of Telangana (ITE&C Department)
summary: Telangana's AI strategy framework launched as part of declaring 2020 the Year of AI with a vision to make Telangana a global hub for AI and achieve USD 5 billion AI contribution to IT exports by 2025. Structured around six pillars: (1) Data Exchange Platform and High-Performance AI Computing — expanding the state open data portal and establishing a shared HPAIC facility with IIT Hyderabad and JNTU Hyderabad and CDAC and introducing data provider certification for ethics and quality of shared datasets; (2) Skilling and Education — targeting 30000 new AI workforce additions by 2022 through AI training centres in tier-II cities and micro-credentials and an AI Summer School and a Foundation of AI for All programme; (3) Governance, Ethics and Privacy — establishing an AI Ethics Group to produce advisory guidelines and codes of practice and governance frameworks covering accountability and bias and transparency and privacy and security and safety and requiring compliance reports from companies using government data; (4) Research and Innovation — including AI innovation cohorts in priority sectors and attraction of global applied AI R&D centres and R&D fellowships and government-priority applied research grants; (5) Enabling Adoption and Community Collaboration — through a GovTech Catalyst programme and corporate-startup matchmaking and an SME AI platform; (6) AI-Innovestment Fund — a humanitarian investment fund for AI for social good in agriculture and healthcare and education and mobility and law enforcement. Established T-AIM (Telangana AI Mission) in partnership with NASSCOM as the central execution body. Includes financial and non-financial incentives for AI startups and MNCs and research organisations.
who_it_applies_to: State government departments and AI companies and startups and academic and research institutions operating in Telangana; IT companies and startups accessing state government datasets; international MNCs establishing AI centres in Telangana; SMEs adopting AI solutions
key_obligations: Companies accessing government datasets must submit a compliance report detailing ethical and appropriate usage of data; employees of all IT companies utilising government-published datasets must complete a mandatory data ethics course; government agencies procuring AI must follow AI procurement guidelines developed by the AI Ethics Group including use of explainable AI and mechanisms for interpretability and accountability; operational staff in government agencies deploying AI must receive training on the capabilities and limitations of the AI solution including understanding when human review of decisions is required; data providers contributing to the open data exchange platform must obtain data provider certification aligned with the forthcoming national Data Privacy Law

title: Karnataka Artificial Intelligence Strategy
issuing_body: Government of Karnataka
summary: Karnataka is developing a dedicated AI strategy to complement its IT and BT and S&T sector policies. The state has referenced AI prominently across its IT Policy 2020-2025 and Startup Policy 2022-2027 and Karnataka Digital Economy Mission. A standalone AI strategy is expected to formalise Karnataka's ambition to position Bengaluru as a global AI hub.
who_it_applies_to: State departments and IT sector companies and startups and GCCs and research institutions in Karnataka
key_obligations: Details pending finalisation; expected to align with IndiaAI Mission pillars and prescribe AI skilling and governance standards for Karnataka-based AI companies and government deployers

title: Tamil Nadu Safe and Ethical Artificial Intelligence Policy 2020
issuing_body: Government of Tamil Nadu (Information Technology Department)
summary: State-level AI policy establishing a mandatory ethical evaluation framework for all government AI procurement and deployment. Introduces the six-dimensional TAM-DEF framework covering Transparency and Audit and Accountability and Legal Issues and Misuse Protection and Digital Divide and Data Deficit and Ethics and Fairness and Equity as the analytical lens for assessing AI systems before public rollout. Mandates the DEEP-MAX scorecard — a seven-parameter point-based rating tool covering Diversity and Equity and Fairness and Ethics and Privacy and Data Protection and Misuse Protection and Audit and Transparency and Cross Geography and Society — for evaluating every AI system procured by government. Proposes an AI Certification, Transparency and Scorecard (ACTS) Blockchain to store tamperproof DEEP-MAX scores and training data certificates for all government AI modules. Establishes a Safe and Ethical AI Monitoring Committee chaired by the Chief Secretary. Assigns TNeGA's Centre of Excellence in Emerging Technologies (CEET) as the technical advisory body for government AI procurement. Sets out capacity-building obligations for citizens and the executive and the legislature and the judiciary. Promotes open data and an AI sandbox and collaborative research centres and expert groups for AI innovation.
who_it_applies_to: All authorities or bodies in Tamil Nadu established under Central or State law and owned or controlled by the Government of Tamil Nadu or receiving aid directly or indirectly from it; all organisational bodies including cooperatives and trusts and societies and public sector undertakings and boards whose composition is controlled by or whose office bearers are appointed by the Government of Tamil Nadu; all partnerships and joint venture companies of the Government of Tamil Nadu
key_obligations: Consult CEET at TNeGA before initiating any AI procurement; evaluate all proposed AI systems against the DEEP-MAX scorecard prior to public deployment and obtain a satisfactory score; record DEEP-MAX scores on the ACTS-Blockchain once operational and on TNeGA's interim mechanism until then; update DEEP-MAX scores at least every six months for all deployed AI systems given their self-learning nature; accept the Government of Tamil Nadu's right to set and periodically revise DEEP-MAX acceptability thresholds and to reject or recall any AI application that does not meet those thresholds

title: AI in Indian Defence: A Compendium of AI-Based Products and Technologies
issuing_body: Department of Defence Production, Ministry of Defence (MoD), DRDO
summary: A 118-page compendium published by the Department of Defence Production, Ministry of Defence in July 2022, showcasing AI-based products and technologies developed by Indian defence industry stakeholders including public and private companies, DRDO, academic institutions, and start-ups. Organised into thematic categories: Human Behavioural Analysis, Unmanned Ground Vehicles and Drones (Sapper Scout mine detection UGV, AI Capability in Swarm Drones, Project Storm autonomous room intervention drone), Autonomous Systems (Autonomous Fast Intercept Boat, AI-Enabled ROV), Cognitive and Electronic Systems (Cognitive Radar, AI-Based Intercept Management System, Adversary Network Analysis Tool ANANT), Surveillance and Reconnaissance (AI-Surveillance System, AI-Enabled Airborne Electro-Optic IR system, Facial Recognition for population monitoring, V-logger vehicle tracking, AI-based 360° monitoring, Segmentation of Satellite Panchromatic Videos), Maritime AI (Autonomous Maritime Anomaly Detection, Machine Algorithms for Maritime Anomaly, AI/Big Data for Acoustic and Magnetic Signature Analysis, AI-based Passive Track While Scan), Cybersecurity (Android Malware Detection, Permissive Blockchain Mechanism), Logistics and Supply Chain (PRO-HM+ AI in SCM), Manufacturing and Maintenance, Intelligent Monitoring Systems (HUMS Ground Station), and Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems. Covers applications across ISR, data management, weapons, and counter-terrorism. Demonstrates the breadth of India's defence AI ecosystem spanning autonomy in weapon systems, counter-terrorism, border protection, and soldier support.
who_it_applies_to: Indian defence industry stakeholders, DRDO, defence PSUs, private sector defence companies, academic institutions, start-ups, armed forces, and policymakers involved in defence AI procurement and capability development.
key_obligations: Informational/compendium document — no binding obligations. Provides a showcase of existing AI capabilities to guide defence procurement, R&D investment decisions, and policy formulation. Companies featured must comply with applicable defence procurement procedures, export control regulations, and DRDO technology transfer agreements.

title: National Digital Health Mission: Health Data Management Policy
issuing_body: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) / National Digital Health Mission (NDHM)
summary: Foundational data governance policy for the National Digital Health Ecosystem (NDHE) establishing the "Security and Privacy by Design" framework for personal digital health data. Adopts a federated architecture for interoperable health data management. Defines the roles and obligations of all entities in the NDHE: data fiduciaries (including hospitals and Health Information Providers), Health Information Users, consent managers, data processors, researchers, payers, and pharmaceutical entities. Establishes the Health ID (digital health identifier linked to Aadhaar or other official ID), Healthcare Professional ID, and Health Facility Registry as the three core identity layers. Sets out a detailed consent framework requiring free, informed, specific, and revocable consent for all personal health data access. Specifies data principal rights including confirmation and access, correction, erasure, restriction, data portability, and nominee designation for emergencies. Mandates privacy by design, purpose limitation, data minimisation, collection limitation, and reasonable security practices for all data fiduciaries. Requires Data Protection Impact Assessments before high-risk processing and strict audit trails for all data access. Includes grievance redressal structure through data fiduciary DPO and NDHM Grievance Redressal Officer. Explicitly prohibits denial of health services for refusal to create a Health ID.
who_it_applies_to: All entities participating in the National Digital Health Ecosystem including: Health Information Providers (hospitals, diagnostic centres, public health programmes); Health Information Users (any entity requesting access to health records); consent managers; data processors acting on behalf of data fiduciaries; health facilities maintaining electronic records; payers (central and state governments, insurers, health plans); pharmaceutical and medical device manufacturers in the health data supply chain; research institutions and individual researchers using health data analytics; Health ID Providers; all NDHM ecosystem partners who collect or process personal health data
key_obligations: Collect or process personal health data only with free, informed, specific, and revocable consent obtained through the NDHM consent framework; issue a clear privacy notice before data collection specifying purpose, categories, and rights; implement Privacy by Design in all system design and business practices; publish a privacy by design policy on entity website; implement reasonable security practices including documented information security programme, de-identification and encryption, and periodic security reviews; conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments before high-risk processing; maintain strict audit trails of all data processing activities; appoint a Data Protection Officer and Grievance Officer and publish contact details; respond to data principal grievances within one month; report data breaches to NDHM; do not use health data beyond the purpose specified in the consent; comply with NDHM-specified anonymisation protocols before sharing or analysing data for secondary purposes

title: Framework for Regulatory Sandbox for Financial Technologies
issuing_body: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
summary: RBI framework enabling fintech companies including AI-driven credit scoring and insurtech and payments startups to test innovative products under relaxed regulatory norms within a defined testing environment with consumer safeguards. Each cohort focuses on a theme with selected entities testing under supervision before full licensing. Has enabled several AI-in-finance proof of concepts.
who_it_applies_to: Fintech companies and banks partnering with fintechs and AI-based lending and insurance and payment platforms seeking to test products before full regulatory compliance
key_obligations: Apply to relevant RBI sandbox cohort with detailed product description and risk assessment and operate strictly within sandbox testing boundary and test only with consenting customers and submit outcome report to RBI at cohort end

title: Consultation Paper on Guidelines for Responsible Usage of AI/ML in Indian Securities Markets
issuing_body: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
summary: SEBI consultation paper issued in June 2025 proposing guiding principles for responsible AI and ML usage across the Indian securities markets. Background draws on SEBI's existing AI/ML reporting requirements for market infrastructure institutions and intermediaries, and the working group's study of Indian and global best practices including NITI Aayog's Responsible AI principles and IOSCO's 2021 AI/ML framework. Documents current AI/ML applications across exchanges (surveillance, cybersecurity, chatbots, pattern recognition), brokers (KYC, product recommendations, order execution, AML), and mutual funds (customer support, segmentation). Proposes five core governance principles: (1) Model Governance — requiring a skilled internal team for model oversight, auditability, explainability and version control, designated senior management accountability, vendor management, periodic revalidation, data governance norms, independent auditing with findings reported to SEBI, and complete verbosity logs retained; (2) Investor Protection and Disclosure — mandatory disclosure to customers of AI/ML use in trading, advisory, and portfolio management, including model risks, limitations, accuracy results, and data quality; (3) Testing Framework — pre-deployment testing in segregated environments including shadow testing, continuous post-deployment monitoring, and minimum five-year documentation retention; (4) Fairness and Bias — ensuring models do not discriminate across client groups and implementing processes to identify and remove data biases; (5) Data Privacy and Cyber Security — clear data security and privacy policies compliant with applicable law and reporting of technical glitches or breaches to SEBI. Proposes a tiered regulatory approach with a lighter framework for internal, non-customer-facing AI uses such as compliance and surveillance. Public comments invited by July 11, 2025.
who_it_applies_to: All SEBI-regulated market participants using AI or ML applications: stock exchanges and clearing corporations and depositories using AI for surveillance and cyber security; stock brokers using AI for KYC, order execution, product recommendations, and AML; asset management companies and mutual funds using AI for customer support and segmentation; portfolio managers and investment advisers using AI in advisory functions; third-party AI vendors providing AI/ML services to capital market entities
key_obligations: Maintain a skilled internal team for AI/ML model lifecycle oversight including auditability and explainability; designate senior management accountable for model governance; conduct pre-deployment testing in segregated environments and shadow testing with live traffic; continuously monitor model performance post-deployment and share accuracy results with SEBI periodically; subject AI/ML systems to independent audits and report audit findings to SEBI; disclose AI/ML usage to customers where it directly impacts them including model risks, limitations, accuracy, and data quality; maintain full-verbosity logs for AI systems; implement data governance policies covering ownership, access controls, and encryption; report technical glitches and data breaches to SEBI; ensure third-party AI vendors are contractually accountable and subject to ongoing oversight

title: India AI Governance Guidelines
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MEITY)
summary: Comprehensive AI governance guidelines developed by a MeitY-constituted drafting committee and released in November 2025. Adopts a techno-legal approach based on three sutras of Trust and People First and Innovation. Establishes risk-based governance obligations across the AI value chain covering developers and deployers and users. Covers content authentication and privacy preservation and bias mitigation and transparency in the AI value chain.
who_it_applies_to: AI developers and deployers and importers and distributors of AI systems across all sectors in India; government entities using AI in public services
key_obligations: Classify AI systems by risk and conduct conformity assessments for high-risk applications and implement content authentication measures for AI-generated outputs and ensure transparency across AI value chain and report significant AI incidents to designated authority

title: National AI Strategy for Skilling and Workforce Development
issuing_body: Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE)
summary: Forthcoming national strategy to prepare India's workforce for an AI-driven economy through PMKVY sector skill councils and integration of AI and ML modules in ITI and polytechnic curricula. Expected to define national AI occupational standards and create a registry of certified AI trainers and link skilling outcomes to AI industry employment.
who_it_applies_to: Sector skill councils and training partners and employers in AI-intensive industries and ITI and polytechnic institutions
key_obligations: Align training curricula with national AI occupational standards upon publication and certify trainers through prescribed process and report enrolment and placement outcomes on SKILL India digital platform

title: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (updated as on 6.4.2023)
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MEITY)
summary: The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021 (IT Rules 2021), published on 25 February 2021 under the IT Act 2000, superseding the 2011 Intermediaries Guidelines. Amended in October 2022 (adding Grievance Appellate Committee) and April 2023 (adding online gaming framework). The consolidated text (updated 6 April 2023) governs three categories of regulated entities. Part II (administered by MeitY): Due diligence obligations for all intermediaries — prominently publish rules, privacy policy, user agreement in user's preferred Indian language; make reasonable efforts to prevent hosting 11 categories of prohibited content including obscene/CSAM material, content threatening national sovereignty, false/misleading information, software viruses, and unverified online real money games; acknowledge user grievances within 24 hours; resolve within 15 days (72 hours for certain content removal requests); remove NCII/morphed images within 24 hours; preserve removed content 180 days; respond to government information requests within 72 hours; report cyber incidents to CERT-In. Additional due diligence for Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) and online gaming intermediaries: appoint India-resident Chief Compliance Officer (CCO), Nodal Contact Person, and Resident Grievance Officer; publish monthly compliance reports; enable traceability of first originator of messages on court/government order; proactively identify CSAM using automated tools with human oversight; enable voluntary user account verification with verification mark; provide pre-removal notification and dispute opportunity for content removed on SSMI's own accord; physical India address required. Online gaming: self-regulatory bodies designated by MeitY verify online real money games as 'permissible'; gaming intermediaries must display verification mark, conduct KYC for real money deposits, prohibit credit financing for gameplay, and disclose withdrawal/winnings policies. Grievance Appellate Committee: government-constituted body to hear appeals from Grievance Officer decisions within 30 days via online dispute resolution. Part III (administered by MIB): Three-tier Code of Ethics for news/current affairs publishers and OTT platforms — Level I self-regulation (publisher Grievance Officer), Level II self-regulatory bodies (headed by retired SC/HC judge), Level III MIB oversight (Inter-Departmental Committee). OTT content classification: U, U/A 7+, U/A 13+, U/A 16+, A ratings with content descriptors; age verification for A-rated content; parental locks for U/A 13+.
who_it_applies_to: All intermediaries operating in India (websites, apps, platforms, social media); Significant Social Media Intermediaries (user threshold notified by Central Government); online gaming intermediaries; publishers of news/current affairs content (online papers, portals, aggregators, agencies); publishers of online curated content (OTT platforms, streaming services). Applies to entities operating in India or conducting systematic business of making content available in India.
key_obligations: Publish rules/privacy policy/user agreement; prevent 11 categories of prohibited content; Grievance Officer (24h acknowledgement, 15-day resolution, 72h for certain NCII/harmful content); preserve removed content 180 days; respond to government requests within 72 hours; report cyber incidents to CERT-In; [SSMIs] CCO/Nodal Contact/Resident Grievance Officer resident in India; monthly compliance reports; traceability on court/govt order; proactive CSAM identification; voluntary account verification; pre-removal notification; [Gaming] KYC for real money deposits; no credit financing; display SRB verification mark; disclose withdrawal policy; [Publishers] Grievance Officer; monthly compliance report; content classification; 60-day record retention.

title: India AI Governance Guidelines: Enabling Safe and Trusted AI Innovation (February 2026)
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
summary: Updated AI governance guidelines released at the AI Impact Summit 2026, building on the November 2025 version. Grounded in seven guiding sutras constituting India's AI governance philosophy: (1) Trust is the Foundation — embedding trust across the full AI value chain; (2) People First — ensuring human agency, oversight, and capacity building; (3) Innovation over Restraint — prioritising responsible innovation over cautionary restriction; (4) Fairness and Equity — designing AI to avoid bias and advance inclusion; (5) Accountability — assigning clear accountability by function, risk, and due diligence; (6) Understandable by Design — ensuring explainability and disclosure as core design features; (7) Safety, Resilience and Sustainability — building safeguards, robustness, and environmental responsibility into AI systems. Presents recommendations across six pillars: infrastructure (expanding compute and data access through IndiaAI Mission, with 38,000+ GPUs onboarded and AIKosh hosting 9,500+ datasets); capacity building (scaling IndiaAI FutureSkills, 570 AI Data Labs, 27 IndiaAI labs); policy and regulation (identifying gaps in existing laws including IT Act, DPDP Act, IT Rules 2021; supporting targeted legislative amendments and regulatory sandboxes); risk mitigation (establishing India-specific AI risk classification framework and national AI incident reporting mechanism); accountability (graded liability proportional to function and risk, transparency reports, accessible grievance redressal); institutions (whole-of-government coordination through proposed AI Governance Group chaired by the Principal Scientific Adviser, Technology and Policy Expert Committee within MeitY, and AI Safety Institute). Provides practical guidelines for industry and regulators including compliance with Indian laws, voluntary adoption of principles, grievance redressal mechanisms, transparency reports, and use of techno-legal solutions.
who_it_applies_to: All persons involved in developing or deploying AI systems in India across all sectors; government ministries and sectoral regulators as policy formulators and enforcers; AI developers, deployers, importers, distributors, and end-users
key_obligations: Comply with all applicable Indian laws and regulations including IT Act, DPDP Act, and IT Rules; demonstrate compliance when called upon by relevant agencies or sectoral regulators; adopt voluntary measures on privacy, security, fairness, non-discrimination, and transparency; create a grievance redressal mechanism for AI-related harms and ensure timely resolution; publish transparency reports evaluating risk of harm in the Indian context or share confidentially with regulators; explore techno-legal solutions such as privacy-enhancing technologies, machine unlearning, and automated bias detection; regulators to prioritise governance interventions where real and present harm or threat to life or livelihood exists; avoid compliance-heavy mandatory approvals unless deemed necessary

title: Strengthening AI Governance Through Techno-Legal Framework
issuing_body: Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India
summary: White paper from the Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser as part of its "India's AI Policy Priorities" series, proposing a techno-legal approach as the appropriate governance model for India's AI ecosystem. Defines the techno-legal approach as the integration of legal instruments, rule-based conditioning, regulatory oversight, and technical enforcement mechanisms to embed compliance directly into AI systems across their lifecycle rather than enforcing rules only after deployment. Identifies five stages of the AI lifecycle requiring distinct risk governance and technical safeguards: (1) Data Collection — risks of privacy breach, safety, intellectual property, security, and fairness; controls include Data Protection Impact Assessments, data classification, consent verification, and privacy threat modelling; (2) Data in Use Protection — risks of unauthorised access, secondary use beyond consent, and bias in training data; controls include privacy-enhancing technologies (differential privacy, synthetic data), confidential computing, and digital contracts for data sharing; (3) AI Training and Model Assessment — risks of model memorisation of personal data, training-time attacks such as data poisoning, and bias embedding; controls include model risk assessment, red-teaming, fairness and explainability scoring; (4) Safe AI Inference — risks of sensitive data disclosure in outputs, hallucinations, prompt injection, and adversarial attacks; controls include prompt-level risk tagging, runtime monitoring, adversarial attack detection, and responsible AI firewalls; (5) Trusted Agents — risks of excessive data access, unauthorised actions, and governance failures in agentic AI; controls include agent identity and authentication, context-based firewalling, behaviour logging, and kill switches. Documents MeitY's national call for responsible AI tools (eight projects selected from universities covering machine unlearning, synthetic data, bias mitigation, explainability, PETs, algorithm auditing, governance testing, and ethical certification) and a second EoI for enforcement-oriented tools including deepfake detection and AI stress-testing. Proposes operationalisation through four institutions: AI Governance Group (AIGG) chaired by the PSA for cross-ministerial coordination; Technology and Policy Expert Committee (TPEC) within MeitY for expert inputs; AI Safety Institute (AISI) for evaluation, testing, and safety research; and a National Database of AI Incidents for post-deployment monitoring. Discusses cross-cutting considerations including privacy-performance tradeoffs, AI-subject vs AI-user governance, deepfake pipeline disruption, cross-border alignment, and capacity building.
who_it_applies_to: AI developers, deployers, and regulated entities across all sectors; sectoral regulators such as RBI, SEBI, and ICMR formulating AI governance frameworks; government ministries and public bodies deploying AI in welfare schemes and public services; academia and industry developing responsible AI tools; AI model importers and distributors
key_obligations: Non-binding white paper; key recommended practices include: implementing techno-legal governance teams within organisations responsible for AI initiatives with board-level ethical accountability; conducting Data Protection Impact Assessments and AI impact assessments before data use in model training; implementing privacy-enhancing technologies and fairness assessment at data collection and training stages; scoring AI models for privacy, safety, security, fairness, and explainability using red-teaming before deployment; deploying responsible AI firewalls and runtime monitoring at inference stage; logging agent behaviour and implementing kill switches for agentic AI; publishing transparency reports and voluntary industry commitments; participating in national AI incident reporting once established; engaging with AIGG and TPEC standard-setting processes

title: Rajasthan Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Policy 2026
issuing_body: Government of Rajasthan
summary: State policy promoting development and responsible deployment of AI and ML across governance and industry.
who_it_applies_to: State government departments and ecosystem partners
key_obligations: Programmatic commitments by state government

title: MahaAgri-AI Policy 2025–2029
issuing_body: Agriculture Department, Government of Maharashtra
summary: State policy and implementation roadmap for deploying AI, Generative AI, and emerging technologies across Maharashtra's agricultural value chain from 2025 to 2029. Aims to address persistent challenges of low productivity, climate variability, water stress, and market inefficiencies while positioning Maharashtra as a national leader in AI-driven agriculture. Built around eight policy pillars: (1) establishing a professionally managed AI and Agritech Innovation Centre under Principal Secretary Agriculture as the central implementation body, complemented by AI Research and Innovation Centres in four State Agriculture Universities; (2) operationalising a federated Agriculture Data Exchange (ADeX) as shared digital public infrastructure with consent-based access and standardised APIs, plus a secure sandbox environment for solution testing; (3) deploying a unified AI-enabled Remote Sensing and Geospatial Intelligence Engine for crop acreage estimation, yield forecasting, drought mapping, and scheme compliance monitoring; (4) implementing the VISTAAR initiative for GenAI-powered multilingual farmer advisory services and simulation tools; (5) building a statewide AI-enabled Agri-Food traceability and quality certification platform using blockchain and QR codes for export-oriented crops; (6) providing differentiated innovation support to agritech startups and established companies through grants, incubation, co-financing, and ADeX access; (7) building institutional capacity in SAUs and training farmers, extension workers, and students; (8) hosting an annual Global AI in Agriculture Conference and Investor Summit. Governance is structured through a State-Level Steering Committee for project approvals and a State-Level Technical Committee for technical and commercial feasibility evaluation. Phased implementation with an initial allocation of Rs 500 crore.
who_it_applies_to: State agriculture departments and district administrations; agritech startups and established companies developing AI solutions; State Agriculture Universities and research institutions; farmers and Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) accessing AI advisory services; exporters and packhouses and certification agencies participating in the traceability platform
key_obligations: Agritech solution providers must submit proposals through the AI and Agritech Innovation Centre and undergo technical and commercial feasibility evaluation by the State-Level Technical Committee before deployment; companies accessing ADeX must comply with consent-driven access protocols and state data governance policies; AI solutions deployed in government schemes must adhere to responsible AI and data privacy standards; participating SAUs must integrate AI and ML training and research into their institutional programmes; all deployed AI interventions are subject to KPI-linked monitoring and third-party impact assessments

title: Responsible AI for All: Adopting the Framework — A Use Case Approach on Facial Recognition Technology
issuing_body: NITI Aayog (research conducted by Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy)
summary: Third paper in NITI Aayog's Responsible AI series, applying the seven RAI principles from Parts 1 and 2 to the specific use case of Facial Recognition Technology (FRT). Part 1 of the paper examines FRT as a concept — how it operates, its rise in use, a taxonomy of non-security and security applications, examples of FRT systems deployed in India and globally, design-based and rights-based risks, and a comparative review of FRT regulation in the EU, UK, USA, Australia, and Canada. Part 2 provides a detailed case study of the Digi Yatra biometric boarding system at Indian airports, evaluating it against all seven RAI principles and the operationalisation mechanisms from Part 2 of the series. Makes actionable recommendations for responsible FRT use both for Digi Yatra specifically and for any future FRT deployment in India, covering law and policy, institutional interventions, technical safeguards, and consent and data minimisation requirements. Research was financially supported by NITI Aayog and conducted by Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy, New Delhi.
who_it_applies_to: Government agencies and private entities deploying facial recognition technology in public or semi-public spaces; civil aviation and airport operators using biometric boarding systems; law enforcement agencies using automated facial recognition; procurers of FRT for identity verification
key_obligations: Ensure FRT use is voluntary and with explicit informed consent; apply all seven RAI principles during design and procurement of FRT systems; conduct bias and accuracy assessments across demographic groups before deployment; implement strict data minimisation and retention limits; establish grievance redressal mechanisms for affected individuals; ensure transparency with affected persons about FRT use; mandate human review of FRT-generated alerts before any consequential action; comply with applicable data protection laws for biometric data

title: Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of Artificial Intelligence in the Financial Sector (FREE-AI)
issuing_body: Reserve Bank of India (RBI) — FREE-AI Committee chaired by Prof. Pushpak Bhattacharyya (IIT Bombay)
summary: A 103-page comprehensive framework report published by the Reserve Bank of India's expert committee on responsible and ethical AI in the financial sector (FREE-AI Committee), constituted in December 2024 under the chairmanship of Prof. Pushpak Bhattacharyya (IIT Bombay). The committee included NITI Aayog, MeitY, HDFC Bank, Microsoft India, and legal experts. The report establishes seven foundational principles (Sutras) for AI governance in finance: (1) Trust is the Foundation — AI must not erode public trust in the financial system; (2) People First — AI augments human decisions but defers to human judgment; (3) Innovation over Restraint — responsible innovation prioritised over cautionary restraint; (4) Fairness and Equity — AI outcomes must be non-discriminatory and promote financial inclusion; (5) Accountability — deploying entities remain fully accountable regardless of automation level; (6) Understandable by Design — explainability as a core design feature; (7) Safety, Resilience and Sustainability — AI systems must be secure and energy-efficient. Organised around two sub-frameworks with six pillars and 26 recommendations. Innovation Enablement Framework — Infrastructure: (Rec 1) establish a publicly governed financial sector data infrastructure integrated with AIKosh; (Rec 2) create an AI Innovation Sandbox for pre-deployment testing; (Rec 3) incentive structures and compute landing zones for smaller entities; (Rec 4) develop indigenous financial sector AI models (LLMs/SLMs) as public goods; (Rec 5) framework for AI-DPI integration. Policy: (Rec 6) adaptive and enabling regulatory policies anchored in 7 Sutras; (Rec 7) regulatory lite approach for AI-driven financial inclusion for underserved segments; (Rec 8) graded liability framework accommodating probabilistic nature of AI. (Rec 9) permanent multi-stakeholder AI Standing Committee under RBI with hub-and-spoke link to national AI Safety Institute. Capacity: (Rec 10) board-level AI competency; (Rec 11) regulator capacity building (potential dedicated AI institute); (Rec 12-13) best practice sharing and recognition programs. Risk Mitigation Framework — Governance: (Rec 14) board-approved AI policy covering governance structure, risk appetite, accountability, auditability, consumer protection; (Rec 15) data lifecycle governance aligned with DPDP Act; (Rec 16) full AI system lifecycle governance including autonomous AI with human oversight for medium/high-risk; (Rec 17) AI-specific product approval framework. Protection: (Rec 18) board-approved consumer protection framework with AI disclosure and grievance redressal; (Rec 19) cybersecurity assessments including red teaming for medium/high-risk applications (minimum semi-annual); (Rec 20) red teaming pre-deployment and after major updates; (Rec 21) AI-specific business continuity plans with fallback mechanisms and human-in-the-loop reviews. Assurance: (Rec 22) AI incident reporting framework with non-punitive reporting culture; (Rec 23) internal AI inventory updated semi-annually and sector-wide AI repository leveraging EmTech Repository; (Rec 24) periodic AI audits (internal for low-risk; third-party for high-risk); (Rec 25) AI disclosures in annual reports covering governance, adoption areas, complaints; (Rec 26) industry-developed AI Compliance Toolkit for voluntary benchmarking.
who_it_applies_to: All RBI-regulated entities (REs) including Scheduled Commercial Banks, NBFCs, All India Financial Institutions, Payment System Operators, FinTechs, insurance companies (IRDAI), capital market entities (SEBI), and technology service providers (TSPs) and third-party AI vendors serving the financial sector. Also addresses financial sector regulators (RBI, SEBI, IRDAI), industry associations (IBA, SROs), academic and research institutions, and cloud/AI infrastructure providers.
key_obligations: Recommendations (non-binding at report stage, to be operationalised through future RBI guidance): Board-approved AI policy; data lifecycle governance aligned with DPDP Act; AI system governance across full lifecycle including model inventory; AI-specific product approval process; consumer protection framework with AI disclosure; red teaming of medium/high-risk applications (at least semi-annually); AI-specific BCP with fallback mechanisms; AI incident reporting; maintain internal AI inventory (semi-annual update); AI-related disclosures in annual reports; participate in sector-wide AI repository; internal/third-party audits based on risk level; voluntary use of AI Compliance Toolkit.

title: Transforming Healthcare Delivery Through Artificial Intelligence
issuing_body: PIB Research Unit, Press Information Bureau, Government of India
summary: A comprehensive PIB Research Unit report released on 13 February 2026, ahead of the India-AI Impact Summit 2026 (16–20 February), documenting the transformation of Indian healthcare delivery through AI from 2022–2025. Key government AI-enabled health programmes: (1) TB Management — Adverse Outcome Prediction (27% decline in adverse TB outcomes) and DeepCXR AI for chest X-ray analysis deployed in 8 states/UTs; (2) Diabetic Retinopathy — MadhuNetrAI enabling non-specialist retinal triage (7,100 patients at 38 facilities; first AI community screening program Dec 2025); (3) Telemedicine — eSanjeevani Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) supporting 282 million consultations with AI-assisted differential diagnosis (April 2023–November 2025), 12 million aided by AI-recommended diagnoses; (4) Traditional Medicine — Ayurgenomics and Ayush Grid integrating AI with Prakriti-based genomics, recognised by WHO July 2025; (5) Cancer Care — NITI Aayog's imaging biobank of 20,000+ patient profiles; (6) Health Fraud — AB-PMJAY Anti-Fraud AI/ML; (7) Surveillance — Media Disease Surveillance (MDS) system issuing 4,500+ outbreak alerts since April 2022. Infrastructure established: AI Centres of Excellence designated at AIIMS Delhi, PGIMER Chandigarh, AIIMS Rishikesh (March 2025); National Federated Learning Platform (MoU NHA-IIT Kanpur, October 2024); ABDM with 799 million digital health IDs (August 2025), 410,000+ registered healthcare facilities, 671 million linked health records. IndiaAI Mission healthcare applications shortlisted include NIDAAN (TB chest X-ray AI), diabetic retinopathy detection, musculoskeletal diagnostics, and cancer staging. Private sector AI contributions showcased (NITI Aayog recognised): NemoCare Raksha (20,000+ newborns), CareNX (500,000+ mothers), Cloudphysician (130,000+ ICU patients), Qure.ai (15 million patients/year), Thermalytix breast cancer screening (75,000+ women). Governance framework: all AI deployment follows ICMR Ethical Guidelines (2023) and MeitY AI Governance Guidelines. MoHFW is developing a sector-specific Strategy for AI in Healthcare for India (SAHI).
who_it_applies_to: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, National Health Authority, NITI Aayog, IndiaAI Mission, AI Centres of Excellence (AIIMS Delhi, PGIMER, AIIMS Rishikesh), healthcare technology companies, diagnostic AI developers, telemedicine platform providers, state health departments, frontline healthcare workers, and policymakers involved in digital health and AI governance.
key_obligations: Informational/advocacy document — no binding obligations. References that all AI health deployments must follow ICMR Ethical Guidelines for AI in Healthcare (2023) and MeitY AI Governance Guidelines. Documents government expectation that AI tools support rather than replace clinical judgment, operate within federated learning architectures for privacy, and integrate with ABDM digital infrastructure. Notes development of SAHI (Strategy for AI in Healthcare for India) as forthcoming binding framework.

title: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules 2025
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
summary: Operationalising rules under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 (DPDP Act), notified by Gazette Notification G.S.R. 846(E) on 13 November 2025 (CG-DL-E-14112025-267650). Phased commencement: Rules 1, 2, and 17–21 (Board governance and appointments) in force from publication date; Rule 4 (Consent Manager registration) in force one year after publication; Rules 3 and 5–16 and 22–23 (core data protection obligations, processing standards, rights, and appeals) in force eighteen months after publication (approximately May 2027). Rule 3 prescribes the form and content of notice from Data Fiduciary to Data Principal: independently understandable notice in clear and plain language itemising personal data and specifying processing purpose; must include links for consent withdrawal, rights exercise, and Board complaints. Rule 4 establishes the Consent Manager regime: entities must apply to the Data Protection Board for registration meeting conditions in First Schedule Part A (India-incorporated company, ₹2 crore net worth, sound management, certified interoperable consent platform); registered Consent Managers must act in a fiduciary capacity, maintain 7-year consent records, avoid conflicts of interest with Data Fiduciaries, publish promoter and ownership disclosures, and submit to Board audits. Rule 5 requires State entities and instrumentalities processing personal data under Section 7(b) of the Act to follow Second Schedule standards. Rule 6 mandates minimum security safeguards: encryption, obfuscation, masking or virtual tokenisation; access controls on computer resources; visibility through logs and monitoring; data backup for continuity; retention of logs and personal data for minimum one year; contractual security provisions with Data Processors; technical and organisational measures for effective observance. Rule 7 governs breach notification: Data Fiduciary must notify each affected Data Principal without delay via user account or registered communication with breach description, consequences, mitigation measures, safety steps, and contact information; must also notify the Board without delay with initial breach details and within 72 hours with full information including causal analysis, findings on breach actor, remedial measures, and report on notifications issued to Data Principals. Rule 8 sets retention and erasure timelines: e-commerce entities with ≥2 crore registered users, online gaming intermediaries with ≥50 lakh users, and social media intermediaries with ≥2 crore users must erase personal data 3 years from last contact with Data Principal for the specified purpose (or Rule commencement, whichever is later), unless law requires retention; must notify Data Principal 48 hours before erasure; all Data Fiduciaries must retain personal data and processing logs for a minimum of one year for purposes in Seventh Schedule (sovereignty, law performance, SDF assessment). Rule 9 requires Data Fiduciaries to prominently publish contact details of the Data Protection Officer or responsible person on their website or app and in every response to Data Principal communications. Rules 10–11 require Data Fiduciaries to adopt technical and organisational measures to obtain verifiable parental consent before processing any personal data of a child; due diligence to verify the parent is an identifiable adult using reliable identity and age details held by the Data Fiduciary or voluntarily provided by the individual or through a virtual token from an authorised entity (including DigiLocker service providers); equivalent obligations for lawful guardians of persons with disability. Rule 12 exempts specified classes of Data Fiduciaries (clinical establishments, healthcare professionals, educational institutions, crèches, transport providers for schools) and specified purposes (state functions in children's interest, email account creation, real-time child location tracking, ensuring age-appropriate access, age verification) from parental consent obligations under Sections 9(1) and 9(3) of the Act. Rule 13 imposes additional obligations on Significant Data Fiduciaries: annual Data Protection Impact Assessment and audit with report to Board; due diligence to verify that algorithmic software used in hosting, displaying, or sharing personal data does not threaten Data Principal rights; implement Central Government committee-directed data localisation restrictions for specified personal data. Rule 14 requires Data Fiduciaries and Consent Managers to publish means for Data Principals to exercise rights; establish grievance redressal mechanism with response within 90 days and appropriate technical and organisational support; enable Data Principals to nominate individuals to exercise rights. Rule 15 permits cross-border personal data transfer subject to Central Government requirements for specific foreign states or entities. Rule 16 exempts research, archiving, and statistical processing from the Act if conducted per Second Schedule standards. Rules 17–21 operationalise the Data Protection Board: Search-cum-Selection Committee processes for Chairperson (Cabinet Secretary-chaired) and Members; consolidated salary of ₹4.5 lakh/month (Chairperson) and ₹4 lakh/month (other Members); Board to function as a digital office using techno-legal measures; officer and employee appointment with Central Government approval per Sixth Schedule terms. Rule 22 provides for digital appeals to Appellate Tribunal with fees equivalent to TRAI Act appeals, payable via UPI. Rule 23 enables Central Government to require Data Fiduciaries or intermediaries to furnish information within specified periods for Seventh Schedule purposes; Data Fiduciaries may be directed not to disclose the furnishing to Data Principals where sovereignty or State security is at stake.
who_it_applies_to: All Data Fiduciaries (government and private entities determining the purpose and means of processing digital personal data of individuals in India or offering goods/services to Indian residents); Data Processors acting on behalf of Data Fiduciaries; Consent Managers applying for Board registration; Significant Data Fiduciaries notified by Central Government; e-commerce entities, online gaming intermediaries, and social media intermediaries meeting user thresholds under Third Schedule; entities processing personal data of children or persons with disability with lawful guardians; Data Protection Board Chairperson and Members and staff
key_obligations: Provide clear, itemised, plain-language notice to Data Principal before consent covering personal data description, processing purpose, and mechanisms for consent withdrawal and rights exercise; [Consent Managers — effective ~November 2026] register with Data Protection Board meeting First Schedule Part A conditions (₹2cr net worth, certified interoperable platform, India incorporation); act as fiduciary to Data Principals; maintain 7-year consent records; publish ownership disclosures; avoid conflicts of interest with Data Fiduciaries; [All Data Fiduciaries — effective ~May 2027] implement minimum security safeguards under Rule 6 including encryption/tokenisation, access controls, monitoring logs, data backups, and 1-year log retention; notify each affected Data Principal without delay upon breach with description, consequences, mitigation, and contact; notify Data Protection Board without delay and submit full breach report within 72 hours; erase personal data when specified purpose is no longer served or consent is withdrawn (Third Schedule entities must erase after 3 years of inactivity; all Data Fiduciaries must retain processing logs minimum 1 year per Seventh Schedule purposes); notify Data Principal 48 hours before scheduled erasure; publish DPO or contact person details prominently on website/app; obtain verifiable parental consent before processing children's personal data using reliable age/identity verification or DigiLocker virtual tokens; verify lawful guardian status for persons with disability; establish grievance redressal mechanism with 90-day response obligation; enable Data Principals to nominate persons to exercise rights; comply with Central Government requirements for cross-border data transfers; [Significant Data Fiduciaries] conduct annual DPIA and audit and furnish report to Board; verify algorithmic software does not threaten Data Principal rights; implement data localisation as directed by Central Government committee

title: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (updated as on 10.02.2026)
issuing_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
summary: Amendment to the IT Rules 2021 by G.S.R. 120(E) dated 10 February 2026, adding a comprehensive synthetic media and deepfake governance framework as the fourth significant update to the rules (after the October 2022 Grievance Appellate Committee amendment and the April 2023 online gaming amendment and the October 2025 content takedown amendment). The consolidated text updated as on 10 February 2026 makes the following substantive changes. First, a new definition of 'audio, visual or audio-visual information' is inserted in Rule 2(ca) to cover any audio, image, photograph, graphic, video, moving visual recording, sound recording or other AV content — whether created, generated, modified or altered through a computer resource. Second, a new definition of 'synthetically generated information' (SGI) is inserted in Rule 2(wa): AI or algorithmically created, generated, modified or altered AV information that appears real, authentic or true and depicts or portrays any individual or event in a manner indistinguishable from a natural person or real-world event; carve-outs exclude routine or good-faith editing, formatting, enhancement, technical correction, colour adjustment, noise reduction, transcription or compression that does not materially alter substance; the routine creation of documents, presentations, PDFs, educational materials, research outputs using illustrative or template-based content that does not produce a false document or false electronic record; and the use of computer resources solely to improve accessibility, clarity, quality, translation, searchability or discoverability without generating or manipulating material content. Third, Rule 1A clarifies that references to 'information' in the context of unlawful acts under Rules 3(1)(b) and 3(2) and 4(2) and 4(4) include SGI. Rule 1B clarifies that removal of SGI for compliance with the rules does not violate the safe harbour conditions under Section 79(2) IT Act. Fourth, Rule 3(c) on periodic user notification is amended from annual to at least once every three months, and is expanded to additionally require intermediaries to inform users that: (i) non-compliance may lead to immediate access termination or content removal; (ii) non-compliance with any law may attract penalty or punishment under the Act or other applicable law; (iii) where a violation constitutes a mandatorily reportable offence under Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 or POCSO Act 2012, users must report to the appropriate authority.
